name: Chavismo
summary: Chavismo is the left-populist, Bolivarian movement built around Hugo Chávez and continued by Nicolás Maduro. It combines nationalism, Latin American integration and anti-imperialism with 'socialism of the 21st century': oil-funded social missions, nationalization, price controls and a communal state of participatory bodies, set against an 'oligarchy' and neoliberalism. It accepts private property alongside social property, and it is socially conservative on abortion and marriage.
scope: The mainstream Chavista project of the Chávez era (1999-2013) as set out in the 1999 Constitution, Chávez's 2005 turn to socialism and the 2012 communal-state speech, with continuity under Maduro. It excludes the pragmatic Delcista turn to reprivatization and the broader pan-Latin Bolivarian family (MAS, Correismo).

universal-healthcare.rationale: The 1999 Constitution makes health a state responsibility and bars privatizing public health assets, and Barrio Adentro clinics were a flagship mission.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Constitution guarantees an annually adjusted vital minimum wage, and raising it regularly was standard practice for the government.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Chavismo defines itself against neoliberalism and 'savage capitalism' and favours state direction of the economy.

public-ownership.rationale: Hydrocarbons are public domain under Article 12, and nationalization of oil, gold, food and other industries was a hallmark policy.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Chávez declared an 'economic war' on the upper classes, but taxation was secondary to oil revenue, so this is inferred.

unions-good.rationale: The Constitution protects union formation and strikes, though the government also sought to steer the labour movement.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property is guaranteed but expropriation for social interest is explicit, and Chávez promoted 'social property' alongside private property.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Price controls, nationalizations and expropriations show a strong preference for tight state control of business.

cut-welfare.rationale: Social missions funded by oil revenue are the core of the project, so adherents reject cutting welfare.

worker-ownership.rationale: Cooperatives, social property and communes are promoted as forms of collective ownership, though state ownership remained dominant.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not a defining issue; inferred from a security-minded, anti-opposition state that treats opponents as conspirators.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Never advocated; inferred from the movement's social conservatism and state-centred approach to public order.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Chavismo labels opponents fascists and has favoured legal curbs on hostile speech; inferred from its record on media regulation.

strong-leader.rationale: Populist and personalist, with enabling acts and a strong presidency central to the movement and its identification with a leader.

state-harmful.rationale: Chavismo expands the state's role in economy and social provision and is the opposite of anarchism.

limit-guns.rationale: Not documented in the sources opened; inferred from a left-populist state favouring strong public order controls.

empower-police-military.rationale: The military was given a role in public order and development, as in Plan Bolivar 2000, and the armed forces are central to the movement.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not a Chavista cause; inferred from the government's recent prudish turn and opposition to liberalizing moral laws.

decide-locally.rationale: Communal councils and communes are meant to shift power to local self-government, though in practice power was centralized.

rehabilitation.rationale: Not directly documented; inferred from a left-populist emphasis on social causes of crime.

traditional-family.rationale: The Constitution protects motherhood and the family, and recent Chavismo courts evangelical constituencies.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Marriage equality was never advanced by the movement and a National Assembly sub-commission opposes it.

abortion-legal.rationale: The Constitution protects life and motherhood and the abortion rules have barely changed; liberalization was shelved under Chávez and opposed since.

more-religion-public.rationale: Chávez invoked Christ as a socialist and Chavismo courts evangelicals, yet the Constitution guarantees religious freedom and the state clashed with the Catholic hierarchy.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Constitutional recognition of indigenous rights and inclusion of the excluded poor reflect commitment to correcting historical exclusion.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not a defining issue; Chavismo is socially mixed and gender theory is not part of its core doctrine.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Bolivarianism stresses patriotic service, national sovereignty and heritage from Bolivar.

gradual-change.rationale: It describes itself as a revolution and a refounding of the republic, not incremental change within established institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Constitution lets resident foreigners vote locally after ten years and the movement favours Latin American integration.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: It prefers regional blocs of states and a multipolar order, and distrusts global institutions such as the IMF and World Bank.

free-trade.rationale: ALBA was created as an alternative to the US-backed Free Trade Area of the Americas, and it favours barter and solidarity trade.

nation-first.rationale: National independence is the first aim, yet the movement is committed to regional integration and cooperation through ALBA.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Non-intervention is a constitutional principle and Chávez opposed Western military interventions as imperialist.

open-borders.rationale: Admission of foreigners is a matter of national power, and no source shows support for open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Oil-funded expansion is central; the later ecosocialist language of the Plan de la Patria is secondary to production goals.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Chavismo rhetoric blames capitalism for climate change but the economy depends on oil, so adherents are split in practice.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No documented stance; adherents emphasize social organization over technology.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not a defining issue and no source opened addresses it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Chávez led the 1992 coup attempt, calls the movement the Bolivarian Revolution and cited Trotsky's permanent revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: The movement stresses protagonistic popular participation over technocratic rule.

central-planning.rationale: Planning and nationalization are favoured over market allocation, though a mixed economy with private property persisted.

socialized-markets.rationale: Chavismo accepts private property and markets alongside social property and cooperatives, so it accepts publicly or worker-owned firms.

land-value-tax.rationale: Not addressed; inferred as no tradition of single-tax thinking in the movement.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not documented; inferred from its hostility to the wealthy and oligarchy.

basic-income.rationale: Missions and cash bonuses exist, but the model favours in-kind missions and work, so adherents are split.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Economic self-sufficiency is a stated Bolivarian aim, implying protection of domestic production.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State control of oil and strategic industries and planning are central.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Land redistribution from big landowners and cooperatives suggest broad ownership, though communal property is preferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Chavismo accepts private property and a mixed economy rather than a moneyless society.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Chavismo favours state control of finance and opposes market liberalism.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not its model; it favours popular power and unions rather than state-recognized corporate bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Constitution declares pluralist elective government and adherents claim an electoral democracy, despite PSUV dominance.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: A republican movement founded on Bolivar's republicanism.

democracy-best.rationale: Chavismo claims to deepen democracy through participation, though it contests opponents' legitimacy.

direct-votes.rationale: Articles 71 to 74 provide consultative, recall and abrogatory referendums as central to participatory democracy.

workers-councils.rationale: Communal councils and communes are bodies of popular power, but they are neighbourhood based rather than workplace councils.

right-to-secede.rationale: Territorial integrity and indivisible national sovereignty are constitutional principles.

natural-rulers.rationale: Populist anti-oligarchic movement that rejects inherited superiority of elites.

political-violence-never.rationale: Chávez defended his 1992 insurrection and speaks of armed revolution, so the movement rejects an absolute ban.

war-builds-character.rationale: Strong patriotic and martial symbolism, but not a doctrine that war strengthens the nation.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion, but the state courts and funds evangelical churches and uses religious rhetoric.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Constitution is secular and guarantees freedom of cult.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The movement is state-centred and rejects privatized security or justice.

military-superiority.rationale: The movement emphasises defence against perceived imperial threats, but this is not framed as superiority over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Constitution recognises indigenous peoples and Bolivarianism celebrates a mixed Latin American identity.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Chávez described himself as Marxist and Trotskyist at times, and the movement frames politics as the people against oligarchy.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Reducing inequality was the stated aim of the missions and of redistribution.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Article 119 grants native peoples collective, inalienable ownership of their lands.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Anti-imperialist and anti-colonial discourse implies sympathy; inferred, not documented as a demand.

civilizational-union.rationale: Latin American union, from Gran Colombia to ALBA and CELAC, is a defining aim.

self-interest-moral.rationale: It opposes 'savage capitalism' and stresses solidarity and collective service.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Bolivarianism stresses a patriotic ethic of service and the Constitution imposes duties, but it also guarantees extensive rights.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental protections appear in the Constitution and the later Plan de la Patria uses ecosocialist language.

limit-population.rationale: No population policy; inferred as Chavismo treats poverty as a social-structure problem.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Blames capitalism, not industry, and aims for development and industrialization.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Stresses popular participation by people, not algorithms.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Inferred from a security-minded state hostile to opposition networks.

restore-past-order.rationale: Presents itself as a revolutionary, forward-looking project even while invoking Bolivar.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Ideological project; early pragmatism gave way to a declared socialist programme.

direct-action.rationale: The movement relies heavily on elections, referendums and recalls to legitimise its rule.

means-match-ends.rationale: The communal state aims to build socialism through popular self-government in the present.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Chavismo is a developmentalist project of missions and modernization.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Missions deliver food, health and education on need, but no stated communist principle.

production-for-use.rationale: Social property and communal economy aim at needs rather than profit, and markets are rejected as the organising principle.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Chávez rejected capitalism as exploitative, but also accepted private enterprise, so this is not an orthodox Marxist doctrine here.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: 21st-century socialism rejects Leninist orthodoxy in favour of democracy and referendums.

collective-farming.rationale: Land reform created cooperatives and state farms alongside redistribution to individuals.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Anti-imperialist framing links capitalism and US power to war, as in Chávez's opposition to the Afghanistan invasion.

taxation-theft.rationale: Rejects libertarian arguments and favours a large redistributive state.

harm-principle.rationale: Inferred from its willingness to limit speech, property and activity for social interest.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Article 119 recognises collective rights of indigenous peoples and social rights are central.

conscription.rationale: Article 134 imposes a defence duty but forbids forcible recruitment.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Popular participation and voting are the centre of its idea of democracy.

state-as-business.rationale: Rejects neoliberal management of the state.

positive-liberty.rationale: Social rights to health, education and work and the missions reflect freedom as material capacity.

media-academia-power.rationale: Chavismo claims private media backed the 2002 coup and wielded oligarchic power.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The movement champions an inclusive, mixed Bolivarian identity and rejects racial hierarchy; inferred.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation is through parties and communal councils, not families or estates.

total-state.rationale: The Constitution declares pluralist government, though the state has a large role.

national-rebirth.rationale: The Bolivarian Revolution is framed as refounding the republic, but not a decadence narrative per se.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Constitution forbids ceding territory and enshrines non-intervention.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: A republic founded on elected, constitutional authority.

bound-labor.rationale: It redistributed land from landowners, the opposite of binding farmers to a lord.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Populist and anti-oligarch narrative holds that elite institutions reflect power; inferred.

universal-morality.rationale: Christian ethical influence on Chávez coexists with relativism about Western claims; split.

single-common-good.rationale: Populist ideology treats the people's will as one common good against an elite.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Chávez's alignment with anti-imperialist Palestinian-solidarity causes; inferred.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: No documented position in the sources.

workplace-democracy.rationale: 21st-century socialism calls for democratic control by those who create value, and cooperatives and co-management were promoted.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Bolivarian missions and schools expand public education.

economic-freedom.rationale: Rejects the claim that political freedom depends on market freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: The Bolivarian national ethic stresses moral example and patriotic service.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Constitution declares independence and untransferable sovereignty, and independence is the first Plan de la Patria objective.

force-without-un.rationale: Principles of non-intervention and opposition to US unilateral wars.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Christian influence and a populist emphasis on feeling and moral rhetoric; inferred.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Missions served residents broadly and the Constitution extends some rights to foreign residents.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Missions are not conditioned on work.

class-collaboration.rationale: Chávez's 'economic war' on the upper classes frames politics as conflict.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Bolivarian heritage and patriotism are central, opposed to destroying inherited institutions.

dominated-front.rationale: ALBA, Petrocaribe, CELAC and TeleSUR were built as a front against US dominance.

workers-nation.rationale: Internationalist, regional integration, with the people framed nationally.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Constitution guarantees equality, though family-focused.

ban-interest.rationale: Freedom of economic activity is guaranteed and there is no usury ban.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Chavismo holds that the old state served oligarchies and must be replaced by a communal state.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Oil is the base of the economy and of its social programs and diplomacy.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Inclusive of foreign residents with local voting rights.

elite-replacement.rationale: No such doctrine; it welcomed regional migration.

proportional-representation.rationale: Not a defining demand; adherents are indifferent.

national-mission.rationale: Chavismo aims to spread the Bolivarian model through ALBA and regional alignment, though non-intervention is also professed.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Left-populist thinking acknowledges gender inequality; inferred.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Anti-corruption and anti-oligarch politics are central to the movement.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Chavismo denounces pre-1999 state violence, but resists accountability for its own forces.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The opposite of the expansive state of Chavismo. The sources do not state this position outright; it follows from the tradition's core commitments.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Bolivar's pan-Hispanic, mixed-heritage idea of the nation.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equality rhetoric is central although the movement divides people between people and oligarchy.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Builds socialism within Venezuela while pursuing regional integration.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: A single secular constitutional order applies to citizens.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Freedom of religion is constitutionally guaranteed.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Constitution guarantees religious freedom, but state schools' role is not documented.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The movement builds state and military strength against perceived US hostility.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Article 5 states that sovereignty resides in the people.

population-transfer.rationale: The Constitution protects rights and forbids such expulsions.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The movement stresses solidarity and rejects competition.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Chavismo labels opponents fascists and has restricted opposition parties; inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: The Constitution creates five branches that cooperate, with Article 136 stating this division.

vanguard-party.rationale: The PSUV is a mass party with a leading role, but adherents are split on vanguard doctrine.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Serving the poor through missions is the central aim.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing missions assign homes to the poor, but there is no stated council-tenant sale policy.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The Constitution recognises the right to strike, though PDVSA strikers were dismissed.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Blames capitalism and oligarchy for poverty, not population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Bolivarian identity is celebrated as diverse and unifying.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: States of exception and enabling acts were used against opposition threats; inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Fixed price ceilings on staple foods since 2003.

party-controls-media.rationale: Formally pluralist media, although the state expanded state media and non-renewed RCTV.

party-commands-army.rationale: Formally the state commands the forces, despite a civic-military union.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Anti-elite and a patriotic ethic of service.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: PSUV is a disciplined mass party.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Article 5 makes sovereignty untransferable and integration is intergovernmental.

head-commands-forces.rationale: A strong presidency in the 1999 Constitution.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Censorship is constitutionally banned, though recent moves against reggaeton show a moralistic trend.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to the Constitution's protections for life and rights; inferred as eugenics is no part of the movement.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Chávez led an armed uprising and the movement rejects a pacifist or libertarian bar on force.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Chávez pushed to end term limits and the 2009 referendum abolished them for all offices.

recall-officials.rationale: Article 72 of the 1999 Constitution makes all elected offices revocable by referendum, and Article 6 describes government with 'revocable mandates'.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The 1999 Constitution bars foreign military bases and the movement opposes US-led alliances, while building its own alliances such as ALBA.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred: the Great Housing Mission gave homes to the poor, but the constitution accepts private property and the movement did not seek to ban renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: Chávez created the Bolivarian Militia as a citizen reserve alongside the armed forces and promoted a civic-military union, rather than abolishing the professional army.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo's land reform and agrarian rhetoric favour the countryside but its base is largely urban poor, and no source makes a moral claim.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Bolivarianism seeks Latin American union of the lands split after independence and Chávez revived the Bolivar's vision of one 'Patria Grande'.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Inferred from the populist contrast of the people with the 'oligarchy' and elites, though the movement also built mass education missions.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The Constitution recognises indigenous peoples' cultures and languages as national heritage, and the movement stresses anti-colonial respect for cultures.

death-penalty.rationale: Article 43 of the Constitution states that no law shall provide for the death penalty and no authority shall apply it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution guarantees equality of the sexes and free education, but the movement's social conservatism and evangelical alliances limit enthusiasm.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo is a secular state project that favours science education, though its evangelical ties give some adherents the opposite view.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred from the socially conservative lean on abortion and marriage and from state media regulation, not from a stated position.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution makes nationality by birth a category and Chavismo has a civic nationalism, so descent-only citizenship is not its stance.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Constitution gives native languages official status for indigenous peoples and requires their use to be respected throughout the territory.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Adherents are split: the Constitution protects religious freedom but no source addresses exemptions from general law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Inferred: the movement stresses collective unity and popular mobilisation over individual nonconformity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Chavismo is anti-neoliberal and anti-imperialist, and Chávez-era foreign policy attacked IMF-style creditor conditions; ALBA stresses solidarity over market finance.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Chavismo holds that national sovereignty requires economic transformation, which is the core of its anti-neoliberal, nationalizing Bolivarian socialism.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The 1999 Constitution was written by an elected National Constituent Assembly, and Chávez made convening it his first act.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement claims participatory democracy and guarantees political rights in the 1999 Constitution, while critics note restrictions in practice.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Bolivarian principles stress solidarity with poor nations, and Venezuela gave oil aid through Petrocaribe.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Chavismo stresses national sovereignty and opposes foreign domination, but no nuclear weapons programme is documented. Inferred from its principles; no source addresses it directly.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The 1999 Constitution provides for the president to be elected by direct, universal vote.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Chavismo subordinated monetary policy to the government, and the 1999 constitution and later practice bring the central bank under state direction.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: No source addresses this; Chavismo has an anti-imperialist outlook but the question is not part of its core. Inferred from its principles; no source addresses it directly.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The 1999 Constitution guarantees property but subordinates it to the general interest, and Chavismo adds social property.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Chávez himself invoked Trotsky and rejected Leninist state models, but the movement is not known to take a position on what the USSR was. Inferred from its principles; no source addresses it directly.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian emphasis on ecology and state protection of the people, though not documented in the sources.

collective-defense.rationale: Chavismo opposes US-led alliances and stresses sovereignty and non-intervention, preferring regional blocs such as ALBA.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Inferred from its anti-imperialism and sovereignty principles, which reject imposed territorial changes.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Inferred from the 1999 constitution’s religious freedom and the movement’s evangelical and socially conservative wing.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Inferred: Chávez led as a partisan figure and the movement does not treat the presidency as above party.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Inferred from Bolivarian emphasis on national sovereignty and integrity.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Inferred from the push for a centralised communal state, which gives regions little separate system.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Inferred from its secular republican, Bolivarian constitutional order.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Inferred from its redistributive socialism and rejection of neoliberalism.

character-from-environment.rationale: Inferred from the socialist project of forming a new person through social conditions, education and missions.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The 1999 constitution binds rulers to law, although critics say Chavismo bent it.

space-expansion.rationale: Inferred: not a Chavista priority, with oil-funded social spending prioritised.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Inferred from its participatory democracy and communal state, which seek popular rather than mixed rule.

leader-cult.rationale: Chávez’s personality cult, with portraits and mass praise, is described in accounts of the movement.

equal-parenting.rationale: The 1999 constitution affirms equality of spouses but custody presumptions are not documented.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Chavista rhetoric casts the revolution as a continuing fight against the oligarchy and 'bureaucratism' inside the state; inferred from that framing, not a stated Marxist thesis.

land-redistribution.rationale: Chávez's 2001 land law and Zamora mission expropriated idle large estates (latifundios) for redistribution to farmers.

refugee-return.rationale: Not a Chavista theme; inferred from its anti-imperialist solidarity with displaced peoples such as Palestinians.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The 1999 Constitution stresses territorial integrity and non-intervention, though it maintains the Essequibo claim on historical grounds, not nationality.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and worship, and Chavismo has no tradition of punishing apostasy.

women-must-cover.rationale: Nothing in Chavismo or the Constitution supports dress mandates; it is a secular-leaning, Christian-majority movement.

common-currency.rationale: ALBA's SUCRE regional virtual currency was created to replace the dollar in trade among members, showing support for a shared regional currency.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Bolivarianism calls for Latin American union across borders, based on shared language, history and heritage.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The Constitution grants indigenous peoples their own institutions, languages and education, but the movement does not address national minorities generally; adherents are split on how far this goes.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Inferred from the movement's emphasis on equal rights within existing states and its solidarity with anti-colonial struggles; not addressed directly.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Chávez drew on Marx and also on Christ, Bolívar and moral appeals, and socialism of the 21st century stresses values and consciousness alongside material change, so adherents are split.

ban-cartels.rationale: Price controls and anti-hoarding laws targeted monopolistic business power, and the Constitution bans monopolies; inferred as a general stance against concentrated economic power.

no-bailouts.rationale: Chavismo favours an active state, and it nationalized and rescued some failing firms and banks; inferred from its interventionism.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Chavismo's participatory populism treats popular sovereignty as supreme, and the movement packed and reshaped the Supreme Court; critics cite this as weakening checks on the majority.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Constitution stresses gender equality and Chavista bodies adopted parity-style candidate rules, though the movement has not made equal representation a defining demand.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Chavismo wants food and economic sovereignty and less dependence on the US, but it also builds trade blocs such as ALBA and relies on oil exports, so it does not seek closure from outside trade.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: ALBA was set up as a trade alternative that puts social welfare and solidarity ahead of free-market rules, so it favours trade terms with social standards.

moral-incentives.rationale: Chávez's 21st-century socialism explicitly draws on Che Guevara and calls for solidarity and a new socialist morality over capitalist profit motives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Chávez led the failed 1992 coup attempt, but after 1998 he took power by election and Chavismo officially advocates a peaceful revolution; adherents are split.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Bolivarianism and the Constitution rest on republican equality and rejection of an 'oligarchy' of inherited elites.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Chavismo builds on a Bolivarian nationalist reading of history centred on Bolívar and Latin American independence, and the 1999 Constitution places Bolivarian ideals at the base of education.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Chavismo is anti-imperialist and rooted in resistance to colonial and US domination, and rejects rule over other peoples.

patriotic-education.rationale: The Bolivarian project stresses national sovereignty and Bolivarian patriotism, and Chavista curricula promote loyalty to the nation and Bolívar's legacy.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Inferred; the 1999 Constitution recognises indigenous rights and the movement's redistribution aims favour measures for disadvantaged groups.

public-money-creation.rationale: Inferred; the government subordinated the central bank to its development aims, though this is not stated as a doctrine of public money creation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Chavismo calls for a socialism of the 21st century to overcome capitalism, which Chávez said could not solve poverty, though it accepts private property and mixed forms.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Inferred; Chavismo promotes Latin American integration and Bolivarian ties across former Spanish-American lands, though these are not an imperial inheritance.

delink-world-market.rationale: Chavismo seeks South-South integration through ALBA and less dependence on the US, but remained tied to oil exports and the world market.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Inferred; Chavismo sees imperial extraction from poor countries but is populist and does not emphasise this class-split claim.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The 1999 Constitution bars discrimination and Chavismo rejects market freedom that overrides equality and social rights.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Chavismo prizes the 1999 Constitution with its extensive rights catalogue, though it sought to amend it in 2007 and 2009 and privileges participatory power over limits.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Inferred from its anti-imperialism and Bolivarian nationalism, which treats colonial-era arrangements as illegitimate.

elective-rulers.rationale: The 1999 Constitution has the people elect the president and all offices, and rejects inherited rule.

minority-veto.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo's majoritarian, plebiscitary style favours decisions by popular majority over minority vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Inferred from the 1999 Constitution's provisions for popular sovereignty and revocable mandates, which imply a right to remove a ruler who betrays it.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Inferred: the system is presidential and Chavista rule concentrated power in the executive, so this has no clear answer.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Inferred from the movement's left-populist humanism; the sources do not discuss animals.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred: the sources are silent on animals and adherents would be indifferent.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Inferred from socialism of the 21st century's solidarity ethic, though it frames the duty as the state's and the people's rather than aristocratic charity.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Chavismo calls for participatory protagonism and the communal state, which expects citizens to take part in public life.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Inferred: Chavista rhetoric attacks the private media as an oligarchic tool that shapes opinion.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Inferred from Chavismo's Gramscian-influenced language of hegemony against the oligarchy and neoliberalism.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Anti-imperialism and ALBA treat the world economy as one that drains the periphery, a core Bolivarian claim.

native-born-offices.rationale: Inferred: the 1999 Constitution reserves the presidency and some posts to Venezuelans by birth, and Chavismo is nationalist.

party-own-road.rationale: Inferred from its principle of national sovereignty and independence from foreign direction.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Inferred from Bolivarian sovereignty and the aim of endogenous, oil-funded development, though ALBA also uses foreign partnerships.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Inferred from Bolivarian nationalism and Venezuela's claim to the Essequibo, which it presents as lost to colonial-era arbitration.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Inferred: the 1999 Constitution recognises indigenous rights, but the movement does not claim rule by one descent group over another.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Inferred from its left, anti-imperialist stance, in which anti-fascism is a standard commitment.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Inferred from the Marxist-influenced left, which rejects the equivalence of communism and fascism.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Inferred: the anti-imperialist left holds the standard view that slavery was the cause, though the sources are silent.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Inferred from the Chávez government's removal of the Columbus statue in 2004 and its anti-colonial symbolism.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Inferred: the sources do not address it, and the movement is socially conservative on gender matters.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Inferred: not covered in the sources, and the movement is socially conservative on gender.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian claim to a sovereign path distinct from neoliberal Western models.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Inferred from the civic-military union, in which the armed forces are partners in the Bolivarian project.

paid-care-work.rationale: Inferred from socialism of the 21st century's social rights agenda, which counts domestic labour as work deserving support.

filial-duty.rationale: Not a Chavista theme; inferred from the movement's social conservatism on family and its communitarian ethos.

office-by-exam.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from Chavismo's preference for popular and party-loyal participation and mission-based appointments over meritocratic exams.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Nationalization of strategic sectors such as oil and telecoms, and the 1999 Constitution's defence of national sovereignty, imply barring foreign takeover of strategic firms.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Not addressed; Chavismo is socially conservative on marriage but nothing in its sources deals with divorce procedure, so adherents are split.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Article 72 makes all elected offices revocable by referendum, and Article 6 describes government as one of revocable mandates; Chávez also stressed leaders obeying the communes.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Chavismo opposes privatization and neoliberal pension models and treats social security as a state responsibility; the 1999 Constitution makes it a public, non-profit service.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Chavismo's socialism of the 21st century favours social and communal property and Chávez's land reform redistributed idle land to those who work it, though private property is still accepted.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1999 Constitution gives the National Assembly the power to approve the budget, which Chavismo wrote in; in practice it dominated that body.

single-official-language.rationale: The Constitution makes Spanish official but also recognizes indigenous languages as official for indigenous peoples, and Chavismo champions their cultural rights.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the Constitution has sovereignty and land provisions but adherents are split on foreign owners, and ALBA integration points the other way.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Chavismo champions Afro-descendant and indigenous rights, but its class-based framing makes an outcome-only test of discrimination uncertain; inferred.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Chávez's socialism criticized capitalist consumption and the culture of the oligarchy, though oil-funded imports supported consumption; inferred.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Chavismo's anti-imperialism extends solidarity to Cuba and leftist movements, but it is mostly rhetorical and sources do not describe a doctrine of arming insurgents.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Chavismo is anti-imperialist and defends national sovereignty, condemning great-power interventions in allied countries; adherents might defend allies, so it is not strongly stated.

corporate-influence.rationale: Chavismo casts the opposition as an oligarchy tied to business and denounces neoliberal capital's hold on politics.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Chavista governments treat NGOs and media funded from abroad as instruments of imperialism, and restrict them.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Inferred from nationalism and a communal-state emphasis on the family; Chavismo has not made pronatalism a central policy.

residents-only-property.rationale: Inferred: the 1999 Constitution protects private property and the state has expropriated land, but residency-based limits are not stated.

job-guarantee.rationale: The 1999 Constitution protects work as a state-protected right and socialism of the 21st century promotes state-supported jobs and missions.

democratic-peace.rationale: Chavismo views Western democracy promotion as cover for imperialism, so it denies that spreading democracy brings peace.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo sees bourgeois law as an oligarchic tool but governs through constitutional legality and asks citizens to obey it.

non-intervention.rationale: Chavismo and ALBA stress sovereignty and non-interference, and the 1999 Constitution upholds non-intervention.

industrial-unions.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo built parallel unions, but the sources do not take a stand on industrial versus craft structure.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo's own conspiracy talk targets oligarchs and the US, not an ethnic or religious minority.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo is socially conservative on marriage and the 1999 Constitution protects marriage.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The 1999 Constitution guarantees citizens access to state information, though Chavista rule has restricted it in practice.

local-production.rationale: Inferred: communal councils and communes aim at local production, and Chavismo promoted food sovereignty.

informal-organisation.rationale: Chavismo builds a communal state of formal bodies and a mass party, not small informal groups.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Chavismo stresses national sovereignty and the 1999 Constitution places Venezuelan law above outside authority.

religious-nation.rationale: Chavismo's nationalism is civic and Bolivarian, not religious, though some Evangelical currents have grown within it.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The Constitution stresses sovereignty and non-intervention, and Bolivarianism opposes foreign hegemony in favour of equal states.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Inferred from the centralised oil-revenue model funding national missions and an ethos of solidarity across the country.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Chavismo recognises private property alongside social property and aims for social ownership of key production, which fits this reading loosely.

defeat-communism.rationale: Chavismo allied with Cuba and other socialist states and framed itself as socialist, so it does not seek to defeat communism.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The Constitution makes health a state duty and bars privatising public health assets, and the missions were state-run.

religion-illusion.rationale: Chávez professed Christianity and evangelical currents exist within Chavismo, so it does not treat religion as an illusion.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Chávez declared capitalism must be transcended and rejected it as the route to a better society.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Inferred from the socialist critique of capitalism; the sources do not link women's equality to economic change directly.

socialized-care.rationale: Inferred from the Constitution's social rights and state-run social missions; domestic work is not directly addressed in the opened sources.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred from Bolivarian anti-imperialism, which focuses on politics and economics rather than language policy.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred from the Constitution's recognition of indigenous rights and its emphasis on legal commitments.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Chávez proposed a communal state built from self-governing communes with social property.

majority-settlement.rationale: Inferred from the Constitution's recognition of indigenous peoples and rejection of minority subordination.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Chávez rejected capitalism and Soviet-style Leninism, calling for a new 21st-century socialism as a different path.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Venezuela asserts a historical title to the Essequibo under the 1999 Constitution's territorial clause, so a historical claim is treated as strong; inferred, not a doctrinal point.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Chavismo's antisemitic rhetoric aside, it has no tradition of Holocaust denial; inferred from its general left-nationalist outlook.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Chavismo has never sought to criminalize homosexuality; its social conservatism is expressed by opposing marriage equality, not by penal law (inferred).

suppress-opposition.rationale: Chavistas present the system as pluralist and denounce repression, though critics document persecution of opponents; an adherent would reject the statement as stated.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The 1999 Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and worship, which is incompatible with punishing blasphemy; inferred from that.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Anti-imperialism and opposition to colonial exploitation are core to Chavismo and the Bolivarian project, so ruling overseas territories for the metropole is rejected.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Chavismo sympathises with anti-imperialist resistance generally but has no position on a religious duty of jihad; treated as neutral.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Chavismo bases legitimacy on popular sovereignty and a secular constitution, not religious law, so it rejects religious grounds for removing rulers (inferred).

participatory-democracy.rationale: The 1999 Constitution provides for participation and protagonism of the people, and Chávez's communal state builds communal councils and communes to give citizens direct decision-making.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Chavismo links class oppression with racial exclusion and recognises Afro-descendant and indigenous rights, but gives priority to class; the intersectional framing is inferred.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The movement is socially conservative on marriage and abortion and has not legislated gender identity recognition; inferred from those positions.

assisted-dying.rationale: Given its social conservatism and ties to evangelical currents, Chavismo is unlikely to back assisted dying; inferred, not a stated position.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Chávez framed politics as the people against the oligarchy and explicitly set his socialism against a 'third way' centrism, so he would reject merging left and right.

alienated-labor.rationale: Chávez's socialism of the 21st century drew on Marxist critiques of capitalism and sought to end exploitation and alienation of workers, though alienation is not a central slogan.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Chavismo's anti-Western, anti-imperialist stance and alliances with Iran make it hostile to such claims; inferred.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Constitution vests sovereignty non-delegably in the people (Art. 5), so authority comes from the people, not God, whatever Chávez's personal religiosity.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: The Constitution protects religious freedom and Chavismo has no tradition of banning religious dress in institutions; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: The Constitution and Chavista labour law stress worker protection against employers; no document addresses NDAs, so this is inferred.

social-market-economy.rationale: Art. 299 of the Constitution allows a mixed economy, but Chavismo rejects the market-led model and favours a much larger state and social property than a social market economy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Chavismo built a civic-military union and militia and sees armed forces as guarantors of sovereignty against imperialism, so it opposes abolishing them.

rich-first.rationale: Egalitarian socialism and opposition to neoliberal inequality make letting some grow rich first unattractive; inferred.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Chavismo seeks a multipolar world and builds ALBA as an alternative bloc, rejecting NATO and US alliances, though it aligns with Russia and China; inferred.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 1999 Constitution fills the presidency by popular election, and Chavismo's legitimacy rests on electoral mandates, not inherited office.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo favours state-run and nationalized finance and social property rather than user-owned mutual banks, though it accepts private banks alongside.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Chavismo is defined by opposition to neoliberalism and imperialism, and Chávez broke with Washington-aligned lenders to set an independent course.

property-franchise.rationale: The 1999 Constitution rests on universal suffrage and participatory democracy, and Chavismo casts itself against an wealthy 'oligarchy', so wealth qualifications are alien to it.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution protects gender equality and the environment and 21st-century socialism is framed as anti-exploitation, but linking the two is not a stated Chavista doctrine.

reification.rationale: Inferred from 21st-century socialism's rejection of capitalist markets, though Chavista texts do not use the concept of reification.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Chavismo denounces the privately owned media as an oligarchic power, and the government refused to renew RCTV's licence and built community and state media.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Constitution sets up the rule of law, but Chávez governed through enabling-law decrees and discretion, and adherents do not clearly side either way.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Constitution guarantees equality and non-discrimination and recognizes indigenous peoples, and Chavismo is a mixed-race popular movement that rejects racial exclusion.

online-participation.rationale: Inferred from Chavismo's stress on direct participation in communal councils; online deliberation is not a stated programme.

open-government-data.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution guarantees access to public information and participation, though government practice has been opaque.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and equality before the law, and Chavismo has not sought to restrict marriage across faiths.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Chavismo's constitutional order forbids discrimination on religion, and it has no tradition of boycotting religious minorities.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Chavismo built communal councils and the communal state as participatory bodies, but sortition is not part of its stated programme; inferred from that participatory ideal.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Chávez presented Christ as a socialist and Chavismo has an evangelical wing that reads faith through liberation-style social teaching; inferred, not a stated doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Chavismo frames the opposition as an oligarchy and pursues redistribution and social property, though the sources do not state the liberty argument. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian emphasis on social inclusion and non-discrimination in the Constitution; the movement is socially conservative in practice, so adherents are not united.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and worship and Chavismo courts religious, including evangelical, support rather than promoting atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The movement stresses state security forces and civic-military unity, and the Constitution provides for police and prisons; abolition is not part of Chavista thinking.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred from the Chavista commitment to majoritarian popular sovereignty against the oligarchy and a unitary state; power-sharing quotas are not discussed in the sources.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Chavismo builds the state-run social missions and communal state as the main anti-poverty tools and rejects charity-based neoliberal approaches.

term-limits.rationale: Chávez pushed the 2009 referendum abolishing term limits on elected office, arguing the people should be free to re-elect leaders.

vote-delegation.rationale: Chavismo favours participatory communal democracy and recall referendums, but delegable proxy voting is not discussed; inferred as neither a goal nor opposed.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; the movement's priorities are present social needs and sovereignty, so this is neither a stated priority nor opposed.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The Constitution guarantees equality, but the movement is socially conservative and engages churches that limit offices to men, so the view is split and inferred.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred from the Constitution's guarantee of equal rights and obligations between spouses, though adherents' social conservatism makes this uncertain.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The 1999 Constitution grants long-term resident foreigners the vote in local elections, as I recall it; not re-checked in this session.

rent-control.rationale: Inferred from Chavista price controls and social missions for housing, though rent caps specifically are not documented in the sources.

abolish-ip.rationale: The Constitution protects intellectual property and authors' rights, and the movement never sought to abolish them.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo has a civic-military doctrine, but the sources document no uniformed youth movement.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian principles of sovereignty and peace and Chávez's anti-imperialism, not from a stated policy.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The Constitution bars foreign military bases, in line with Bolivarian sovereignty and anti-imperialism.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred from the movement's anti-imperialist and indigenous-rights positions; the issue is not discussed in the sources.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Socialism of the 21st century rejects capitalism and favours social property and labour-based income, while accepting some private property.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo glorified armed struggle and a civic-military role, and rejects pacifism.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Inferred from the cult of Bolívar and the founding narrative that the Bolivarian Revolution continues independence-era struggle.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Inferred from the movement's social conservatism on marriage and abortion.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo is socially conservative on marriage and gender and does not adopt deconstructionist feminism.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian cult of fallen heroes and Chávez himself, with religious imagery in popular Chavismo.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Inferred from the movement's moral struggle against 'oligarchy' and imperialism with religious language.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Inferred: Venezuela is not a diaspora homeland and Chavismo ties the nation to its territory and state.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred: the Bolivarian project begins with the constituent power and state transformation, not prior cultural renewal.

god-not-male.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo has taken no known stance on gendered language for God; it is indifferent.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Inferred from the movement's social conservatism and its alliance with evangelical believers.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The Constitution declares Venezuela multi-ethnic and recognises indigenous rights; Chavismo opposes oligarchy but not on ethnic lines.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution recognises indigenous territories but Chavismo has no programme to merge regions by people.

independent-unions.rationale: The 1999 Constitution protects union freedom, but the movement set up the pro-government UNT and pushed unions to align with the revolution; inferred from that practice.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Chávez's 21st-century socialism and the communal state claim to give power to organised communities and workers rather than to the state alone.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The Constitution keeps public health assets public and declares waters public domain, and the missions expanded state-run services.

second-chamber.rationale: The 1999 Constitution replaced the Senate with a unicameral National Assembly, a founding Chavista reform.

municipal-property.rationale: Chavismo recognises social and communal property alongside state, private and mixed property, but the state keeps the commanding assets, notably oil.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The communal state was built with central direction and funding from Caracas, not as bottom-up confederations whose delegates only coordinate.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred from the constitutional right to a salary sufficient for a dignified life for the worker and family.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Inferred from its state-centred health model and preference for regulation over risk-taking market speed.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: No stated position; the movement backs state science funding but has not prioritised life extension.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Inferred from the exchange and capital controls imposed from 2003, which put payments under state control.

online-anonymity.rationale: Inferred from Chavista media-regulation laws and the movement's distrust of opposition media, which favour state oversight of online speech.

person-over-state.rationale: The Constitution (Article 3) says the state exists to defend and develop the person and respect human dignity, though the movement also stresses collective ends.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Chávez invoked Christ and Chavismo has an evangelical wing, but the movement itself is secondary on spiritual themes.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Despite federal language, Chavismo recentralised power and created parallel communal bodies under the national government; inferred from that record.

gm-crops.rationale: Inferred from its food-sovereignty and anti-corporate agriculture stance, which is hostile to multinational seed control.

dense-cities.rationale: No stated position, and adherents have not engaged with the environmental case for density.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Chavismo recognises indigenous and Afro-Venezuelan rights but frames politics around class and the people against the oligarchy, not racial parties.

racial-pride.rationale: Chávez celebrated mixed, indigenous and Afro-Venezuelan heritage as part of Bolivarian national pride; inferred.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The Constitution commits foreign policy to peaceful settlement and non-intervention, and Chavismo is anti-imperialist and condemns aggression.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Inferred from the Bolivarian vision of a united Latin America sharing language and history across state borders.

communal-electorates.rationale: Inferred from the Constitution's single national citizenry and electorate; separate religious electorates are foreign to it.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Chavista anti-imperialism holds that the United States and local oligarchs conspire against Venezuela, as in the 2002 coup attempt.

free-public-college.rationale: The 1999 Constitution makes public education free through undergraduate level, and Misión Sucre expanded university access.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Inferred from oil-funded extractivism and state-led development; the sources do not address pollution taxes.

future-generations.rationale: The 1999 Constitution frames environmental protection as a duty for the benefit of present and future generations.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Chavismo promoted women's inclusion in missions and the Constitution but no source frames women as bringing distinct values; adherents are split.

arms-reduction.rationale: Inferred from the civic-military union and the creation of a national militia, which stress arming the people over disarmament.

open-diplomacy.rationale: No source addresses this; ALBA stressed sovereignty and solidarity, but adherents are not clearly committed either way.

capital-controls.rationale: The Chávez government imposed exchange and capital controls in 2003 as part of state control of the economy.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Chavismo armed civilian militia and tolerated pro-government colectivos, so a strict state monopoly is not its practice; the 1999 Constitution does assign defence to the armed forces.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The doctrine of civic-military union and Bolivarian defence against imperial threat means soldiers are expected to serve the revolution; inferred.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The 1999 Constitution protects labour rights including collective bargaining and Chavismo sided with workers against employers; the movement also sought to control unions.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Chavismo relied on direct social missions and price controls rather than tax credits; no stated position.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Chavismo opposed neoliberal austerity and used oil-funded spending without binding borrowing limits.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Anti-imperialism and a multipolar order are central, and ALBA was created as an alternative to US-led trade arrangements.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Chavez's 2012 communal-state speech calls for dismantling the inherited bourgeois state and building a communal one in its place.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Chavismo offered a model of socialism of the 21st century yet allowed social and private property side by side, with communes as local experiments.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Chavez blamed capitalism for ecological destruction; the view that nature should be priced as capital is inferred to be rejected.

sacred-nation.rationale: Bolivarian nationalism venerates Bolivar and the fatherland as a lasting community; inferred from Bolivarianism.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Free education missions and state action to widen access suggest support, inferred from the social missions.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Chavismo's anti-oligarchy politics casts rich elites exploiting the poor, and exploitation of the periphery by the core, in colonial terms.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Humanist, Christian-socialist rhetoric and the 'new man' idea point to shared dignity, though the 'new man' implies reshaping; inferred.

public-service-media.rationale: Chavismo expanded state media and used regulation against private broadcasters; independence from government was not a goal.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Not addressed; Chávez was Catholic and evangelical currents have joined Chavismo, but it has no doctrine on religious truth.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from the agrarian reform, price controls and state food programmes of the Bolivarian project.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Article 129 of the Constitution commits the state to preventing nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, and Venezuela holds none.

workers-own-party.rationale: Inferred from the movement's appeal to working people against the 'oligarchy'; Chavismo built its own party, the PSUV, rather than relying on the old ones.

ban-fgm.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; inferred from the Constitution's equality guarantees and the state's social-rights framing.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Article 88 guarantees equal treatment of men and women in work and recognises housework as economic activity; land inheritance is not discussed.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Not addressed; Article 9 makes Spanish official with indigenous languages recognised, but the question is not a Chavista issue.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution handles the environment through state duty and regulation (Articles 127-129), not private liability suits.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Articles 119-126 recognise indigenous peoples' own social and political organisation, but give no advisory chiefs' role in national law.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Article 127 makes protecting the environment a right and duty of each generation, and 21st-century socialism puts social goals above individual freedoms.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; no clear Chavista position on fixed sentencing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Article 9 makes Spanish official, but Chavismo's welcoming stance to migrants and its focus elsewhere leave no clear position.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Inferred from the movement's pro-labour stance and the Constitution's protection of free unionization; compulsory union dues are not something Chavismo set out to abolish.

voter-id.rationale: Inferred from Venezuela's biometric, ID-based voting system, which the government defends as the guarantee of a clean vote.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and worship on equal terms and keeps the state from favouring a faith.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Constitution defines democracy as participatory and protagonistic, with social rights and recall, so elections alone are not enough.

premarital-sex.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo is conservative on abortion and marriage but has not campaigned to censure women's sex outside marriage.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Inferred from the government's record of blocking sites and throttling access in crises, which adherents defend as protection against destabilization.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Inferred from the missions model of separate state programmes, which Chavismo would not fold into one cash payment.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Constitution grants suffrage and eligibility to all citizens and bans discrimination on grounds of sex.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Inferred from the movement's ties to liberation theology and evangelical supporters, who see religion as supporting women.

race-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from Chávez's celebration of a mixed Venezuelan people and the Constitution's ban on racial discrimination.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: The Constitution commits the state to equality of women, and the government created a women's ministry and institute.

homestead-ownership.rationale: The 1999 Constitution allows private property but subordinates it to social function, and Chavismo expropriated land and enterprises that were idle.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo's anti-imperialism led it to distrust Western-led international courts; the sources do not address them directly.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: Chávez invoked Christ and an evangelical strand exists, but the movement is not committed to biblical literalism.

gendered-self-government.rationale: The 1999 Constitution recognises Indigenous rights and guarantees gender equality, and uses gender-inclusive language throughout.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo built a statist socialism and would defend it against capitalist restoration and foreign attack, framed as defence against imperialism.

indirect-election.rationale: The communal state envisaged communal councils feeding into higher bodies by delegates, as in Chávez's 2012 communal-state speech.

national-church-status.rationale: The 1999 Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and equality of faiths, with no established church.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Inferred: the 1999 Constitution recognises Indigenous peoples' habitats and lands, but the unitary Bolivarian state favours communal over regional autonomy.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo upholds Venezuelan sovereignty claims such as Essequibo, which it would not put to inhabitants' vote.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Inferred: Bolivarianism stresses Latin American unity, and Venezuela defends its inherited borders, including the Essequibo claim.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred: Chavismo promoted oil-funded consumption and social missions rather than austerity or self-sufficiency.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred: the Constitution protects Indigenous lands, but the sources do not address restricting outside settlement.

equal-conscription.rationale: Inferred: the 1999 Constitution has gender equality and military service obligations, but the sources do not settle conscription of women.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Bolivarian nationalism stresses sovereignty and the inheritance of the liberators, but the sources do not frame it as a spiritual bond with ancestral land; inferred from that nationalism.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The 1999 Constitution protects the right to life and bars the death penalty, and Chavismo presents itself as a rights-based movement; killing without trial is outside its programme.

close-ties-china.rationale: Chavismo sought allies against US influence, and China became a major oil buyer and lender; inferred from its anti-imperialist multipolar foreign policy.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The Constitution stresses non-intervention and self-determination, so state backing for co-nationals abroad is not a Chavista theme; inferred.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The Constitution makes subsoil resources property of the nation and Chavismo frames oil wealth as belonging to all Venezuelans; the compensation idea itself is inferred.

self-ownership.rationale: Chavismo subordinates private property to social property and the social interest; inferred from its socialism of the 21st century.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Chavismo did not make consumption taxes an issue and its governments changed the VAT rate in both directions; adherents have no settled line.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Chavista social rights and missions are framed as universal entitlements, such as health care as a state duty, though missions were aimed at poor areas; inferred as leaning against targeting.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Chavismo praises direct participation through communes and communal councils over mediating institutions, though it runs its own party and strong leader; inferred.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Anti-oligarchy rhetoric opposes privileged business elites, though state-linked firms later enjoyed favours; inferred from the stated stance.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The Constitution guarantees religious freedom and the state is not tied to a denomination, and Chavismo is not organised on denominational lines; inferred.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Chavismo did not address this pairing; it mixes modernising state projects with appeals to national tradition, so adherents have no clear line.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Chavismo is socially conservative on abortion and marriage, but the 1999 Constitution has gender equality language; the divorce question itself is inferred.

national-resource-control.rationale: The 1999 Constitution declares subsoil resources the property of the nation and Chavismo nationalised oil and other sectors and asserted control of PDVSA.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Chavismo seeks to redistribute oil wealth and land towards the poor, and the 1999 Constitution's social rights and Chávez's land reform judge distribution by equality of outcome rather than origin.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; inferred from Chávez's anti-neoliberal, anti-finance rhetoric and ALBA's alternative to global financial institutions.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Not addressed directly; the Constitution recognises indigenous rights and Chávez framed the movement against oligarchic exclusion, so racism is not treated as solved.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; Chavismo stresses the sovereign people's constituent power and revolutionary legitimacy, which does not map onto natural law.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; Chavismo's productive-economy and communal-labour focus gives no clear view on automation.

multipolar-world.rationale: Chávez championed a multipolar world against US hegemony, and ALBA and Latin American integration were built as a counterweight to US power.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Chávez drew on Marxism and socialism of the 21st century, but no source states a position on value theory; inferred.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Chavismo fuses Bolivarian nationalism and sovereignty with an anti-oligarchy politics for the poor.

material-over-identity.rationale: Chavismo is socially conservative on abortion and marriage, which fits the statement, but it also champions indigenous and Afro-descendant rights; adherents are split and this is inferred.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Chavismo rejects markets as the organising principle and the PSUV is not a communist party, though private property is accepted alongside social property; inferred.

missingStatements.text: A president should be allowed to stand for re-election without limit.
missingStatements.rationale: The 2009 referendum abolished term limits for all public offices with 54 percent, after the 2007 reform failed.

missingStatements.text: Elected officials, including the president, should be removable by a recall referendum during their term.
missingStatements.rationale: Article 72 makes all elected offices revocable by referendum, and Article 6 calls government one with 'revocable mandates'.

notes: Positions are those of the Chávez-era mainstream; Madurismo is harder-line and Delcismo more pragmatic on markets. Several social answers are low confidence because the movement avoided these debates and sources are secondary.
